summary: Provides guidelines for allocating OSI NSAP addresses in the Internet. It was on the standards track and was replaced by RFC 1629.

eli5.summary: This gives rules for handing out one kind of network address so they do not clash.

questions: how to allocate osi nsap addresses
how should osi nsap addresses be allocated hierarchically
what is an area address in osi routing
why is address hierarchy important for routing scalability
how do regionals assign addresses to sites
subtitle: How to assign OSI network addresses so routing scales to millions of networks.

tldr.problem: The Internet is growing toward supporting OSI, but without a clear strategy for allocating NSAP (network service access point) addresses hierarchically, routing tables will become too large to manage as the network scales.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC provides guidelines for assigning NSAP address prefixes based on network topology and routing hierarchy, allowing regional and backbone networks to allocate addresses to their customers and advertise them using a single prefix.
tldr.outcome: Operators can reduce routing data by summarizing many address blocks into one prefix, which is essential for scaling to millions of routing domains. However, OSI was superseded by IP-based technologies before these guidelines were widely deployed.

today: RFC 1237 was a Proposed Standard on the standards track but was superseded by RFC 1629. Although these guidelines for OSI NSAP allocation were well-thought-out, OSI protocols never achieved widespread deployment in the Internet. TCP/IP remained dominant, and IPv6 eventually addressed the address space limitations that drove this work. The RFC remains a historical reference for OSI-based network architecture.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: The Internet is transitioning toward a multi-protocol environment that includes OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) protocols alongside TCP/IP. To support OSI in the Internet, an OSI lower-layers infrastructure is required, including the Connectionless Network Protocol (CLNP) and supporting routing protocols. This RFC provides guidelines for allocating NSAP addresses (network service access point addresses) in the Internet in a way that allows routing to scale efficiently.
sections.eli5: The Internet needs rules for how to number computers and networks using OSI addresses, so that routers can keep track of where everything is.

sections.title: OSI Routing and Address Structure
sections.content: OSI routing is divided into three parts: ES-IS (end-system to intermediate-system) for local links, intra-domain IS-IS routing for routing within a domain, and inter-domain routing between domains. The intra-domain IS-IS protocol uses a two-level hierarchy: Level 1 routers know the topology within their area, and Level 2 routers maintain the backbone and know how to reach different areas. NSAP addresses are structured as an Initial Domain Part (IDP), a Domain Specific Part (DSP), a High-Order DSP (HO-DSP), a System Identifier, and an NSAP Selector. The HO-DSP plus IDP form the area address, which identifies where a system is located in the network hierarchy.
sections.eli5: OSI has two kinds of routers: some know everything in their neighborhood (Level 1), and some connect neighborhoods to each other (Level 2). Addresses are broken into parts: a part that says what organization manages it, a part that says what region, a part that says what network, and a part that says which computer.

sections.title: Hierarchical Routing and Data Abstraction
sections.content: The key insight is that addresses should be assigned along topological boundaries, not organizational boundaries, to enable routing data abstraction. When a regional network assigns addresses from its own prefix to all its attached customer sites, the regional can advertise all those customers to the backbone using a single summarized prefix. Without this hierarchy, each site would need its own entry in backbone routing tables, causing routing tables to grow as the number of routing domains increases. GOSIP Version 2 defines a hierarchical NSAP structure with Administrative Authority (AA) fields that allow this abstraction at multiple levels. The greatest gains in data reduction occur at the lowest levels of the hierarchy, where the number of nodes is greatest.
sections.eli5: If a big network gives all its customers addresses that start with the same digits, it can tell other big networks 'anything starting with these digits comes through me.' That saves everyone from having to remember every single customer separately.

sections.title: Recommended Address Administration Hierarchy
sections.content: The RFC recommends that addresses be assigned hierarchically according to network topology. For the U.S. Internet, NSAP addresses should primarily be based on two formats: GOSIP Version 2 (using AFI 47 and IDI 0005) and the ANSI DCC=840 format. Backbones should be assigned unique Administrative Authority (AA) identifiers. Each regional or mid-level network connected to a backbone should be assigned an AA or RD (Routing Domain) identifier under the backbone's prefix. Each site connected to a regional should be assigned an area identifier under the regional's prefix. This creates a natural hierarchy where the backbone advertises a few prefixes to international peers, each regional advertises its customers using one regional prefix, and sites organize their own internal addresses. The RFC specifically recommends against regionals allocating addresses from backbone prefixes, as the benefit is small and regionals should remain independent of any particular backbone.
sections.eli5: The backbone has a few big prefixes. Each regional has a prefix based on its backbone connection, and hands out smaller pieces to its customers. Each site has even smaller pieces for its own networks. This way, nobody has to remember everything.

sections.title: Multi-Homed and Special Cases
sections.content: Organizations attached to multiple regionals or backbones (multi-homed domains) present special challenges because they cannot fit neatly into a single hierarchical branch. The RFC discusses four possible solutions: assigning a single independent prefix and accepting routing table entries in multiple backbones; using a separate prefix for each attachment point; assigning a single primary prefix with secondary addresses for other attachments; or using separate prefixes for specific pairs of attachments. Each solution has different trade-offs in terms of routing efficiency, configuration complexity, and failure recovery. Zero-homed domains (organizations with no connection to a public network) must still use globally unique addresses if they might later connect to the global Internet. Private point-to-point links between organizations do not require hierarchical address abstraction, as routing information across them is not propagated to the global Internet. Address transition procedures must account for the possibility that topology changes may require address changes.
sections.eli5: If a company connects to two different networks, it is tricky. Different rules work better for different situations. The RFC explains the choices and their trade-offs.
